strengths: Addresses a fundamental bottleneck in multi-exposure HDR fusion: real-world dynamic HDR datasets are difficult to collect and historically restricted to tiny sample sizes (typically ~100 samples). S2R-HDR provides 24,000 HDR frames across 1,000 sequences with diverse object motions, camera shakes, and lighting scenarios.

The rendering pipeline in Unreal Engine 5 is thoughtfully implemented to output linear HDR data in floating-point EXR format, avoiding irreversible tone-mapping and quantization artifacts, while incorporating realistic camera jitter.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrating that pre-training on S2R-HDR consistently improves downstream real-world performance across multiple model backbones (e.g., SAFNet, SCTNet, HDR-Transformer) in both supervised fine-tuning and unsupervised test-time adaptation settings.

The dual-branch adapter (shared vs. transfer branch) with uncertainty-guided dynamic scaling effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting of synthetic priors while adapting to real-world domain shifts.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty of the proposed S2R-Adapter is somewhat incremental, as the architecture (dual shared/transfer low/high-rank branches) and the uncertainty-based mean-teacher test-time adaptation formulation are closely adapted from prior visual domain adaptation works (e.g., ViDA [24]).

Details regarding the synthetic LDR generation pipeline are briefly discussed: realistic camera pipelines involve non-linear camera response functions (CRFs), sensor noise (read/shot noise), and clipping artifacts across exposures. More analysis on how closely the simulated LDR degradations match real raw/sRGB capture characteristics would strengthen the paper.

The evaluation on real data is confined to relatively small benchmark test splits (e.g., 36 scenes for SCT and 27 for Challenge123). While these are standard benchmarks, a structured user study assessing perceptual realism and deghosting quality on open-domain captures would provide stronger evidence.
Minor presentation omission: the repository URL in the abstract ends abruptly ('Dataset and code will be available at').

strengths: Addresses a fundamental bottleneck in deep learning-based HDR deghosting/fusion: existing real-world dynamic HDR datasets are severely constrained in size (typically fewer than 150 scenes) and dynamic range variation.

The S2R-HDR dataset is well-designed, leveraging Unreal Engine 5 to produce 24,000 raw linear HDR frames (EXR format) that bypass standard game engine tone mapping and gamma correction, while incorporating realistic elements such as camera shake, diverse lighting conditions, and dynamic agents (humans, animals, vehicles).

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple representative architectures (both CNN-based such as SAFNet and Transformer-based such as SCTNet and HDR-Transformer) and multiple real benchmarks (SCT, Challenge123, Kalantari, Real-HDRV).

Provides a unified adaptation scheme (S2R-Adapter) covering both supervised adaptation with ground truth and test-time adaptation (TTA) on unlabeled real images via a mean-teacher framework, showing noticeable quantitative and qualitative improvements.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty in the adaptation framework: the dual-branch architecture (low-rank sharing branch, high-rank transfer branch, uncertainty-based weighting, and mean-teacher update) is largely directly adopted from ViDA (Liu et al., 2023) rather than being fundamentally redesigned for low-level restoration.

Lack of detailed modeling of sensor-specific physical degradation: real multi-exposure capture often involves differing motion blur due to varying shutter speeds and non-linear camera response functions (CRFs). The LDR synthesis pipeline primarily uses exposure scaling and additive Gaussian noise, leaving out potential capture artifacts like realistic noise profiles or exposure-dependent blur.

Zero-shot generalization on certain datasets (e.g., SCT in Table 4) exhibits a noticeable domain gap (34.89 dB vs. 42.55 dB trained directly on SCT), indicating that the synthetic-to-real gap remains significant without adaptation or fine-tuning.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental bottleneck in multi-exposure HDR imaging: the scarcity and lack of diversity in existing dynamic HDR datasets with ground truth, which typically contain only ~100 scenes.

The construction of the S2R-HDR dataset is well-motivated, using Unreal Engine 5 to generate 24,000 linear HDR frames (EXR format) spanning varied dynamic elements (pedestrians, vehicles, animals) and diverse lighting conditions.

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple network backbones (SCTNet, HDR-Transformer, SAFNet) and benchmarks (SCT, Challenge123), demonstrating consistent quantitative and qualitative gains when using the synthetic dataset for pre-training.
The paper is generally well-structured and includes extensive supplementary material detailing scene distributions, ablation analyses, and visual comparisons.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty in the domain adaptation component: S2R-Adapter closely follows the formulation and dual-branch design (low-rank shared branch, high-rank transfer branch) of existing parameter-efficient test-time adaptation works such as ViDA (Liu et al., 2023), with standard mean-teacher updates and uncertainty estimation.

Oversimplified physical camera and exposure simulation: In real-world multi-exposure capture, exposure time differences induce exposure-dependent motion blur (long exposure frames experience substantial motion blur, while short exposures are sharp but noisy). S2R-HDR synthesizes multi-exposure LDRs by simple scaling/tone curve manipulation with additive Gaussian noise, ignoring sensor noise models (shot + read noise) and differential motion blur across brackets.

Substantial zero-shot domain gap: As shown in Table 4, zero-shot evaluation on real benchmarks yields significantly degraded performance (e.g., dropping from ~42.6 dB down to ~34.9 dB on SCT), demonstrating that synthetic-only training still exhibits a large domain discrepancy that requires real-domain supervision or adaptation to recover.

Missing comparisons with established domain adaptation / TTA baselines: In the unlabeled test-time adaptation setting (Table 3), S2R-Adapter is not compared against standard source-free domain adaptation or TTA methods (e.g., TENT, CoTTA, or standard LoRA fine-tuning under pseudo-labels), making it difficult to isolate the benefit of the specific adapter structure over other adaptation strategies.
Minor presentation issues: Table 1 caption reads 'Qualitative comparison and analysis...' despite presenting quantitative numerical metrics; code and dataset hosting repositories are left blank.

strengths: Addresses a long-standing bottleneck in learning-based HDR fusion: Existing dynamic HDR fusion datasets with ground truth are tiny (typically around 100 scenes), which severely limits model capacity and generalization. Providing a realistic 24,000-frame synthetic dataset (S2R-HDR) is a valuable and timely contribution to the community.

Well-engineered rendering pipeline: The authors carefully preserve linear HDR floating-point data (avoiding baked-in tone-mapping and quantization), simulate realistic handheld camera shake using Perlin noise, and capture rich dynamic entities (humans, animals, vehicles) under diverse lighting conditions.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments demonstrate clear improvements across both CNN-based (SAFNet) and Transformer-based (SCTNet, HDR-Transformer) architectures on multiple standard benchmarks (SCT, Challenge123, Kalantari, Real-HDRV), showing strong cross-dataset generalization and video temporal consistency.

Effective sim-to-real adaptation framework: The S2R-Adapter approach effectively tackles both supervised fine-tuning and unsupervised test-time adaptation (TTA) via a mean-teacher architecture with uncertainty-guided branch scaling, mitigating catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty in the adapter architecture: The dual-branch adapter structure (low-rank share branch and high-rank transfer branch) and uncertainty-driven dynamic weighting strongly follow existing test-time adaptation paradigms, specifically ViDA (Liu et al., 2023a). The algorithmic contribution is primarily an application of these concepts to HDR fusion rather than a fundamentally new adaptation mechanism.

Simplistic sensor noise and ISP simulation: While floating-point linearity and camera motion are modeled thoughtfully, real raw sensor noise (e.g., heteroscedastic Poisson-Gaussian noise, dark current, hot pixels) and camera optical characteristics (lens flare, blooming, chromatic aberration) are either simplified to basic Gaussian noise or omitted, which remains a primary source of the sim-to-real domain gap in HDR imaging.

Minor presentation issues in figures and formulas: Figure 4 and Figure 5 appear to have duplicated diagram sub-elements (the T-SNE / adapter diagrams are repeated across both figures). Additionally, the exact loss formulation used by the student network during test-time adaptation in Section 4 is only described qualitatively rather than formally stated.

strengths: Addresses a prominent bottleneck in multi-exposure HDR fusion: existing dynamic real-world datasets with ground truth are tiny (typically under 150 scenes) due to the immense physical challenge of capture without motion artifacts or exposure constraints.

The S2R-HDR dataset is large (24,000 frames across 1,000 sequences at 1080p), rendered in linear 32-bit floating point format (EXR) without baked-in tone mapping, and provides diverse foreground motions (humans, vehicles, animals), realistic lighting regimes, and auxiliary ground truths (optical flow, depth, normals).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple real-world benchmarks (SCT, Challenge123, Kalantari, Sen, Tursun) demonstrating that pre-training on S2R-HDR provides strong generalization improvements over training purely on existing small real-world datasets.

Addresses the simulation-to-real domain gap through both supervised adaptation and test-time adaptation (TTA), showing that the proposed S2R-Adapter and uncertainty-based weighting mitigate knowledge forgetting while adapting to real sensor distributions.
weaknesses: The technical novelty of the adaptation framework is somewhat incremental; the dual-branch low-rank / high-rank adapter design and the uncertainty-guided mean-teacher TTA formulation heavily follow existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning and test-time adaptation literature (e.g., ViDA).

Formatting and layout glitches are present in the PDF, especially on pages 5 and 6 where portions of the test-time adaptation teacher-student diagram from Figure 5 appear duplicated/overlapping beneath Figure 4.

The camera sensor noise simulation is relatively basic (additive Gaussian noise on the low/middle exposures), whereas real dynamic low-light / high-exposure raw data exhibits Poisson-Gaussian (shot + read) noise distributions and non-linear sensor response characteristics before demosaicing.

strengths: Addresses a crucial bottleneck in HDR fusion research: the severe scarcity of dynamic training data with ground truth (existing dynamic benchmarks typically contain only 80–150 scenes). The proposed S2R-HDR dataset scales this up significantly to 24,000 HDR frames across 1,000 sequences with diverse lighting, motion, and object types.

Comprehensive dataset engineering: avoids default engine tone mapping and gamma compression to preserve linear HDR floating-point data (EXR), incorporates realistic camera shake simulations, and provides auxiliary modalities including optical flow, depth, and surface normal maps.

Solid empirical results across multiple architectures (CNN-based SAFNet, Transformer-based SCTNet and HDR-Transformer) and multiple real-world benchmarks (SCT, Challenge123, Kalantari, Real-HDRV). Pretraining on S2R-HDR combined with the adapter leads to consistent improvements over training purely on real datasets.

Thorough ablation study validating the individual components of the adapter (low-rank shared branch, high-rank transfer branch, learned vs. uncertainty-guided scale factors) in both supervised fine-tuning and test-time adaptation (TTA) setups.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty of the adaptation framework is relatively limited: the dual-branch adapter (low-rank shared vs. high-rank domain transfer) and uncertainty-driven test-time adaptation heavily borrow from existing works in parameter-efficient fine-tuning and test-time adaptation (e.g., ViDA, Liu et al., 2023a). Its application to HDR fusion is practical, but algorithmically incremental.

Simplistic camera sensor noise modeling: the domain gap between rendered UE5 images and real multi-exposure images is handled in the rendering pipeline by adding simple additive Gaussian noise to lower exposures. Realistic sensor noise characteristics (e.g., heteroscedastic Poisson-Gaussian noise, clipping, and camera-specific response behaviors) are not systematically simulated, which is a key factor in raw/LDR-to-HDR fusion.

Formatting and editorial oversights: Figure 12 is a flowchart describing the generation pipeline but is captioned 'Distribution of optical flow directions across S2R-HDR', which is identical to the caption of Figure 13. Furthermore, Figure 5 contains an orphaned text artifact ('l_style(I_t, I_goal)') in the top-left corner, and Figure 4 and Figure 5 duplicate parts of the block diagrams.

Licensing and asset distribution clarity: the authors mention that several commercial Unreal Engine 5 scene assets were purchased to build the scenes. Clarification on how these assets affect dataset redistribution and licensing for the broader research community would strengthen the submission.
